title: Areas Related to Circles
summary: Chapter 11 of NCERT Class 10 Mathematics covers 'Areas Related to Circles'. This chapter builds upon students' understanding of circles by introducing concepts of sector and segment areas, lengths of arcs, and combinations involving circles. The chapter explains how to calculate areas of sectors and segments using formulas involving central angles and radii. It also covers applications of these concepts in real-life situations and combinations with other shapes. The chapter emphasizes the relationship between the area of a circle, its radius, and the constant pi. Students learn to derive and apply formulas for area and circumference of circles, sectors, and segments, and solve problems involving these concepts in various contexts.

sections.heading: Introduction to Circles and Basic Formulas
sections.para: A circle is a collection of all points in a plane that are equidistant from a fixed point called the center. The distance from the center to any point on the circle is called the radius. The area of a circle is given by A = πr^2, where r is the radius. The circumference or perimeter of a circle is given by C = 2πr or C = πd, where d is the diameter. These fundamental formulas form the basis for understanding more complex concepts related to circles. The constant π (pi) is approximately 22/7 or 3.14 and represents the ratio of the circumference to the diameter of any circle. Understanding these basic formulas is essential before moving on to more advanced topics like sectors and segments.
points: The radius of a circle is the distance from the center to any point on the circle
The diameter is twice the radius and passes through the center of the circle
The area of a circle is calculated using the formula A = πr^2
The circumference of a circle is calculated using C = 2πr or C = πd
The value of π is approximately 22/7 or 3.14
π is a constant ratio of circumference to diameter for all circles
Circles with equal radii are congruent circles
The circumference of a circle is approximately 3.14 times its diameter

keyTerms.meaning: A closed shape where all points are equidistant from a fixed center point
The distance from the center of a circle to any point on the circle
The longest chord of a circle passing through the center, equal to twice the radius
The perimeter or boundary length of a circle
The constant ratio of circumference to diameter of any circle, approximately 22/7 or 3.14

sections.trick: Remember 'Area = πr squared' by visualizing the radius extending out to form a square with area r^2, then multiplying by π.
sections.examPointer: CBSE often asks for direct application of area and circumference formulas with 1-2 mark questions. Remember to use π = 22/7 when radius is a multiple of 7 for exact answers.

sections.heading: Area of Sector and Segment of a Circle
sections.para: A sector of a circle is the portion of a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc. The area of a sector is proportional to the central angle subtended by the arc. For a central angle θ in degrees, the area of sector is (θ/360) × πr^2. A segment of a circle is the region bounded by a chord and the arc subtended by that chord. The area of a minor segment is the area of the corresponding sector minus the area of the triangle formed by the chord and the two radii. For a central angle θ, the area of segment is (θ/360) × πr^2 - (1/2) × r^2 × sinθ. These formulas are essential for solving problems involving circular segments and sectors in various contexts.
points: A sector is the portion of a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc
The area of a sector is proportional to its central angle
For central angle θ in degrees, sector area = (θ/360) × πr^2
A segment is the region bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc
The area of a minor segment = sector area - area of triangle
For central angle θ, segment area = (θ/360) × πr^2 - (1/2)r^2 sinθ
The area of a major segment = area of circle - area of minor segment
When θ = 180°, the segment becomes a semicircle

keyTerms.meaning: The portion of a circle enclosed by two radii and an arc
The region bounded by a chord and the arc subtended by that chord
The angle subtended by an arc at the center of the circle
A portion of the circumference of a circle
A straight line joining any two points on the circumference of a circle

sections.trick: Remember sector area formula as 'fraction of circle' where fraction = θ/360°. For segment, visualize 'sector minus triangle'.
sections.examPointer: CBSE commonly asks 3-4 mark questions requiring calculation of sector and segment areas. Pay special attention to when angles are given in radians versus degrees and ensure proper unit conversion.

sections.heading: Length of an Arc
sections.para: The length of an arc of a circle is proportional to the central angle subtended by that arc. For a circle with radius r and central angle θ in degrees, the length of the arc is given by (θ/360) × 2πr or (θ/360) × πd, where d is the diameter. If the central angle is given in radians, the arc length is simply rθ. This relationship is derived from the fact that the entire circumference corresponds to a central angle of 360 degrees or 2π radians. Understanding arc length is crucial for solving problems involving circular paths, rotations, and various real-life applications where portions of circles are involved.
points: The length of an arc is proportional to its central angle
For central angle θ in degrees, arc length = (θ/360) × 2πr
For central angle θ in radians, arc length = rθ
The entire circumference corresponds to θ = 360° or 2π radians
Arc length can be calculated using either degrees or radians
When θ = 360°, arc length equals the circumference
When θ = 180°, arc length equals half the circumference
Arc length is always measured in linear units (cm, m, etc.)

keyTerms.meaning: The distance along the curved line forming part of the circumference of a circle
A unit of angular measure where one radian is the angle subtended at the center by an arc equal in length to the radius
The relationship between arc length and central angle where arc length ∝ central angle

sections.trick: Remember arc length as 'fraction of circumference' where fraction = θ/360°. For radians, simply multiply radius by angle.
sections.examPointer: CBSE may ask 2-3 mark questions on arc length, often in combination with other concepts like area of sector or in word problems involving circular motion.

sections.heading: Areas of Combinations of Plane Figures
sections.para: In many real-world situations, we encounter combinations of circles with other geometric shapes like triangles, rectangles, or other circles. To find the area of such combinations, we need to identify the individual components and calculate their areas separately, then add or subtract as appropriate. For example, the area of a circle inscribed in a square is found by subtracting the area of the circle from the area of the square. Similarly, the area of a circle circumscribed around a triangle involves finding the area of the triangle and the area between the triangle and the circle. These problems require careful analysis of the given figure and application of appropriate area formulas for each component.
points: Combinations of figures require identifying individual components
Area of combination = sum or difference of individual areas
For a circle inscribed in a square, area = square area - circle area
For a circle circumscribed around a triangle, find triangle area and annular region
When circles overlap, find area of intersection separately
For semicircles attached to rectangles, calculate rectangle area plus semicircle area
For sectors attached to triangles, add their areas appropriately
Always draw clear diagrams to identify all components

A figure drawn outside another figure touching it at vertices

sections.examPointer: CBSE commonly asks 4-5 mark questions on combinations of figures. These questions require careful diagram analysis and step-by-step calculation. Practice identifying all components and their relationships.

sections.heading: Areas Related to Circles in Real Life
sections.para: The concepts of areas related to circles have numerous practical applications in everyday life. In architecture and construction, circular designs are common, and calculating areas of sectors and segments is essential for material estimation. In agriculture, circular irrigation systems require area calculations for water distribution. In transportation, circular roads and roundabouts need area calculations for planning. The design of gears, wheels, and other mechanical components involves circular segments. Even in sports, the playing areas of some sports like cricket involve circular segments. Understanding these applications helps students appreciate the relevance of mathematical concepts in real-world scenarios and enhances problem-solving skills.
points: Circular designs in architecture require area calculations for material estimation
Agricultural irrigation systems use circular patterns for water distribution
Transportation planning involves circular roads and roundabouts
Mechanical components like gears and wheels use circular segments

Circular gardens and parks need area calculations for landscaping

Circular dining tables need area calculations for seating arrangements

sections.examPointer: CBSE includes real-life application questions worth 3-4 marks. These often involve word problems requiring conversion of real situations into mathematical models using circle area concepts.

sections.heading: Conversion of Units and Calculations
sections.para: When solving problems related to areas of circles, it's essential to handle units correctly. Areas are always measured in square units like cm^2, m^2, etc. When converting between different units, remember that 1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m^2 = 10,000 cm^2. Similarly, 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 km^2 = 1,000,000 m^2. For calculations involving π, it's important to use the appropriate value as specified in the problem—either 22/7, 3.14, or the π button on a calculator. When dealing with exact values, it's often better to leave answers in terms of π rather than approximating. Always show all steps in calculations to avoid errors and ensure partial credit even if the final answer is incorrect.
points: Areas are measured in square units (cm^2, m^2, etc.)
Use π = 22/7 when radius is a multiple of 7 for exact answers
Use π = 3.14 when specified or for approximate answers
Leave answers in terms of π when exact value is required
Show all calculation steps to avoid errors
Check units at each step of the calculation

sections.trick: Remember unit conversion for area: 'square the linear conversion factor' - if 1 m = 100 cm, then 1 m^2 = 100^2 cm^2 = 10,000 cm^2.
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently includes unit conversion questions worth 1-2 marks. Always check if the answer needs to be in specific units and show conversion steps clearly. Pay attention to whether exact or approximate value of π is required.

sections.heading: Cost Calculations Involving Circular Areas
sections.para: In many practical applications, we need to calculate the cost associated with circular areas. This includes costs for flooring, painting, fencing, or covering circular surfaces. To find the total cost, first calculate the area that needs to be covered or enclosed, then multiply by the cost per unit area. For example, to find the cost of paving a circular ground, calculate the area of the circle and multiply by the cost per square meter. When dealing with sectors or segments, calculate their areas first, then apply the cost per unit area. For combinations of shapes, find the total area to be covered and then multiply by the appropriate cost rate. Always ensure that units are consistent throughout the calculation.
points: Cost calculations require finding area first, then multiplying by cost per unit area
For circular grounds, cost = area × cost per square unit
For sectors, calculate sector area first, then apply cost rate
For combinations, find total area to be covered, then calculate cost
Ensure units are consistent (area in m^2, cost per m^2, etc.)
For fencing, use circumference instead of area
For painting, only consider the surface area to be painted
Break down complex shapes into simpler components for cost calculation

sections.examPointer: CBSE includes cost calculation questions worth 3-4 marks. These often involve multi-step problems requiring area calculation followed by cost application. Pay attention to whether the entire area or only parts need to be covered.

sections.heading: Problem-Solving Strategies
sections.para: Solving problems related to areas of circles requires a systematic approach. First, carefully read the problem and identify what is given and what is asked. Draw a clear diagram to visualize the situation, marking all given information. Identify the relevant formulas needed for the solution. If dealing with combinations of figures, break them down into simpler components whose areas can be calculated. For problems involving sectors or segments, determine whether you need to find areas, arc lengths, or both. Set up equations if necessary and solve step by step, showing all working. Finally, check if the answer makes sense in the context of the problem and verify units. Practice with a variety of problems to develop proficiency.

sections.examPointer: CBSE values problem-solving strategies in 3-5 mark questions. Even if you can't get the final answer, showing correct methodology and partial working can earn significant marks. Practice with a variety of problems to build confidence.

sections.heading: Common Errors and Precautions
sections.para: When solving problems related to areas of circles, students often make certain errors that can be avoided with proper precautions. One common mistake is confusing the formulas for area and circumference. Remember that area involves r^2 while circumference involves r. Another error is mixing up degrees and radians when calculating sector areas and arc lengths. Always check the unit of the angle given. Students also frequently forget to convert units properly, especially when dealing with areas. It's important to square the linear conversion factor when converting area units. Forgetting to use the correct value of π as specified in the problem is another common error. Always double-check calculations, especially when working with fractions and π.
points: Don't confuse area formula (πr^2) with circumference formula (2πr)
Always check if angle is in degrees or radians before using formulas

Show all working to avoid calculation errors

mcqs.question: If a and b are two prime numbers, then their HCF is
mcqs.explanation: The HCF of two distinct prime numbers is always 1 because they have no common factors other than 1.

mcqs.question: The decimal expansion of 17/8 will terminate after how many decimal places?
mcqs.explanation: The denominator 8 = 2^3, which is of the form 2^m × 5^n where n = 0. So the decimal terminates after m = 2 places.

mcqs.question: If the quadratic equation x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0 has equal roots, then the value of k is
mcqs.explanation: For equal roots, discriminant D = 0. Here D = (-6)^2 - 4(1)(9) = 36 - 36 = 0, so k = 9.

mcqs.question: The sum of first 15 terms of an AP is 105. The first term is 1. The common difference is
mcqs.explanation: Using S_n = n/2 [2a + (n-1)d], we get 105 = 15/2 [2(1) + 14d], which gives d = 1.

mcqs.question: In triangles ABC and DEF, if ∠A = ∠D and AB/DE = AC/DF, then the triangles are similar by
mcqs.explanation: The SAS similarity criterion requires two sides in proportion and the included angle equal, which matches the given information.

mcqs.question: The distance between points (3,4) and (6,8) is
mcqs.explanation: Using distance formula: sqrt[(6-3)^2 + (8-4)^2] = sqrt[9 + 16] = sqrt(25) = 5.

mcqs.question: If sinθ = 3/5, then cosθ is
mcqs.explanation: Using sin^2θ + cos^2θ = 1, we get cosθ = sqrt(1 - (3/5)^2) = sqrt(1 - 9/25) = sqrt(16/25) = 4/5.

mcqs.question: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point on the ground is 30°. If the height of the tower is 30m, the distance of the point from the tower is
mcqs.explanation: Using tan30° = height/distance, we get 1/√3 = 30/distance, so distance = 30√3 m.

mcqs.question: The length of the tangent drawn from a point 8cm away from the center of a circle of radius 6cm is
mcqs.explanation: Using Pythagoras theorem: tangent length = sqrt(8^2 - 6^2) = sqrt(64 - 36) = sqrt(28) = 2√7 cm.

A solid cylinder of height 10cm and radius 7cm is melted and recast into cones of height 2cm and radius 1cm. The number of cones formed is
mcqs.explanation: Volume of cylinder = π × 7² × 10 = 490π cm³. Volume of each cone = (1/3) × π × 1² × 2 = (2/3)π cm³. Number of cones = 490π / (2/3)π = 735.

mcqs.question: The mean of the following data is 15: 10, 15, x, 20, 25. The value of x is
The median of the data 3, 1, 5, 2, 4, 6, 0, 8 is
The empirical relation between mean, median and mode is
mcqs.explanation: The empirical relation is mode = 3 median - 2 mean, which holds for moderately skewed distributions.

mcqs.explanation: There are 26 red cards in a deck of 52 cards, so probability = 26/52 = 1/2.

mcqs.question: If the probability of an event is 0.7, then the probability of its complementary event is
mcqs.explanation: The probability of complementary events sums to 1, so P(complement) = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3.

The quadratic equation x^2 + 7x + 10 = 0 has roots
mcqs.explanation: Factorizing: x^2 + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5) = 0, so roots are x = -2 and x = -5.

In ΔABC, DE || BC and AD/DB = 3/5. If AC = 5.6 cm, then AE is
mcqs.explanation: By Basic Proportionality Theorem, AE/EC = AD/DB = 3/5. Let AE = 3x, EC = 5x. Then 3x + 5x = 5.6, so x = 0.7. Thus AE = 3×0.7 = 2.1 cm.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sqrt(5) is irrational.
boardQuestions.answer: Let us assume, to the contrary, that sqrt(5) is rational. Then we can write sqrt(5) = p/q where p and q are coprime integers and q ≠ 0. Squaring both sides, we get 5 = p²/q², so p² = 5q². This shows that p² is divisible by 5, and hence p is divisible by 5 (since 5 is prime). Let p = 5r for some integer r. Then (5r)² = 5q², so 25r² = 5q², which simplifies to 5r² = q². This shows that q² is divisible by 5, and hence q is divisible by 5. But this contradicts our assumption that p and q are coprime. Hence, our assumption that sqrt(5) is rational is false. Therefore, sqrt(5) is irrational.

boardQuestions.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 12, 15 and 21, and verify that HCF × LCM = Product of the numbers.
boardQuestions.answer: Prime factorization: 12 = 2² × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7. HCF = product of lowest powers of common primes = 3. LCM = product of highest powers of all primes = 2² × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420. Product of numbers = 12 × 15 × 21 = 3780. HCF × LCM = 3 × 420 = 1260. Product of numbers = 3780. Since HCF × LCM = Product of the numbers, the verification is complete.

boardQuestions.question: Solve the quadratic equation 2x² + x - 6 = 0 by factorization method.
boardQuestions.answer: We factorize 2x² + x - 6 as (2x - 3)(x + 2) = 0. Setting each factor equal to zero: 2x - 3 = 0 or x + 2 = 0. So x = 3/2 or x = -2. Therefore, the roots of the equation are x = 3/2 and x = -2.

boardQuestions.question: The sum of four consecutive terms of an AP is 32 and the ratio of the product of the first and the last term to the product of two middle terms is 7:15. Find the terms of the AP.
boardQuestions.answer: Let the four consecutive terms of the AP be a - 3d, a - d, a + d, a + 3d. Sum = (a - 3d) + (a - d) + (a + d) + (a + 3d) = 4a = 32, so a = 8. Product of first and last term = (a - 3d)(a + 3d) = a² - 9d² = 64 - 9d². Product of middle terms = (a - d)(a + d) = a² - d² = 64 - d². Given ratio: (64 - 9d²)/(64 - d²) = 7/15. Cross-multiplying: 15(64 - 9d²) = 7(64 - d²). Simplifying: 960 - 135d² = 448 - 7d². So 128d² = 512, giving d² = 4, so d = ±2. Therefore, the terms are either 2, 6, 10, 14 or 14, 10, 6, 2.

boardQuestions.question: In ΔABC, DE || BC such that AD = 4 cm, DB = 6 cm and AE = 5 cm. Find EC.
boardQuestions.answer: Since DE || BC, by Basic Proportionality Theorem (BPT), we have AD/DB = AE/EC. Substituting the given values: 4/6 = 5/EC. Simplifying: 2/3 = 5/EC. Cross-multiplying: 2 × EC = 3 × 5, so 2EC = 15, giving EC = 7.5 cm.

boardQuestions.question: Find the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining (2, -3) and (-4, 5) in the ratio 3:2.
boardQuestions.answer: Using the section formula, the coordinates of the point dividing the line segment joining (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) in the ratio m:n are ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)). Here, (x₁, y₁) = (2, -3), (x₂, y₂) = (-4, 5), m = 3, n = 2. So x-coordinate = (3×(-4) + 2×2)/(3 + 2) = (-12 + 4)/5 = -8/5. y-coordinate = (3×5 + 2×(-3))/(3 + 2) = (15 - 6)/5 = 9/5. Therefore, the coordinates of the point are (-8/5, 9/5).

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = 1 - 2cos²θ.
boardQuestions.answer: Starting with the left side: sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = (sin²θ)² - (cos²θ)² = (sin²θ - cos²θ)(sin²θ + cos²θ). Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, we get (sin²θ - cos²θ)(1) = sin²θ - cos²θ. Now, sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ, so substituting: (1 - cos²θ) - cos²θ = 1 - 2cos²θ. Therefore, sin⁴θ - cos⁴θ = 1 - 2cos²θ.

boardQuestions.question: A kite is flying at a height of 50m above the ground. The string attached to the kite is temporarily tied to a point on the ground. The inclination of the string with the ground is 60°. Find the length of the string, assuming that there is no slack in the string.
boardQuestions.answer: Let AB be the height of the kite (50m) and AC be the length of the string. The angle of inclination is ∠C = 60°. In right triangle ABC, sin60° = AB/AC. So √3/2 = 50/AC. Therefore, AC = 50 × 2/√3 = 100/√3. Rationalizing, AC = (100√3)/3 m. Hence, the length of the string is (100√3)/3 m.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
boardQuestions.answer: Let O be the center of the circle and P be a point on the circle. Let PT be the tangent at P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to PT. Assume, to the contrary, that OP is not perpendicular to PT. Then there exists a point Q on PT such that OQ is perpendicular to PT. Since Q lies on the tangent PT and Q ≠ P, Q must lie outside the circle. So OQ > OP (as OP is the radius to P). But OQ is perpendicular to PT, so OQ is the shortest distance from O to PT. Therefore, OQ < OP, which contradicts our earlier statement that OQ > OP. Hence, our assumption is false, and OP must be perpendicular to PT. Therefore, the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

boardQuestions.question: Find the area of the shaded region in the figure, where ABCD is a square of side 14cm and APD and BPC are semicircles.
boardQuestions.answer: Area of square ABCD = side² = 14² = 196 cm². Diameter of each semicircle = side of square = 14cm, so radius = 7cm. Area of one semicircle = (1/2)πr² = (1/2)(22/7)(7)² = (1/2)(22/7)(49) = 77 cm². Area of two semicircles = 2 × 77 = 154 cm². Area of shaded region = Area of square - Area of two semicircles = 196 - 154 = 42 cm². Therefore, the area of the shaded region is 42 cm².
